## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with hypertension based on statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Notably, the direct enrichment of regulation of blood pressure (Gene Ontology:0008217, p = 1.44 × 10−8, 21 associated proteins) strongly supports that the prioritized protein set captures core mechanisms controlling vascular tone, fluid balance, and circulatory homeostasis. This is complemented by the phenotype terms hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002615, p = 1.80 × 10−2, 17 proteins) and orthostatic hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0001278, p = 4.53 × 10−2, 9 proteins), suggesting that many of the same molecular regulators contribute to blood pressure instability across both hypertensive and hypotensive states, consistent with literature showing shared involvement of endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and altered vasoactive signaling.

A second major theme is inflammation and immune activation. The very strong enrichment of overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WikiPathways:5095, p = 4.22 × 10−18, 39 proteins), neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p = 7.35 × 10−15, 67 proteins), and signaling by interleukins (Reactome:R-HSA-449147, p = 3.66 × 10−8, 53 proteins) indicates that inflammatory cytokine networks and innate immune cell activation are central to the hypertension-associated signature. This agrees with extensive literature showing that interleukin signaling, leukocyte recruitment, and neutrophil-derived proteases and oxidants promote endothelial injury, vascular stiffness, renal sodium retention, and sustained elevation of arterial pressure. The enrichment of viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, p = 7.44 × 10−20, 35 proteins) further reinforces the importance of cytokine-receptor systems, even though this pathway is annotated in an infectious context.

A third prominent component involves extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue fibrosis. External encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p = 4.46 × 10−39, 93 proteins), collagen metabolic process (Gene Ontology:0032963, p = 2.91 × 10−9, 18 proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p = 4.63 × 10−15, 34 proteins), and carbohydrate binding (Gene Ontology:0030246, p = 5.06 × 10−15, 29 proteins) together point to marked alterations in matrix composition, proteoglycan interactions, and cell-surface adhesion biology. These findings are highly relevant because vascular fibrosis, collagen accumulation, and remodeling of the arterial wall are well-established drivers of increased vascular resistance and reduced compliance in hypertension. The associated enrichment of lysosome (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04142, p = 1.41 × 10−9, 28 proteins) also fits with literature linking lysosomal processing to inflammatory turnover, matrix degradation, and vascular remodeling.

Finally, tissue-enriched signals from placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (Human Protein Atlas:0381223, p = 6.13 × 10−7, 26 proteins) and duodenum; endocrine cells[greater than or equal to Low] (Human Protein Atlas:0151291, p = 2.99 × 10−7, 50 proteins) may reflect specialized secretory and barrier-associated proteins that participate in endocrine, inflammatory, and vascular regulation. The placental signal is particularly notable given the established relationship between placental dysfunction, endothelial injury, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, while the endocrine cell signal may point to hormone-mediated regulation of vascular and metabolic homeostasis. Overall, the pathway pattern supports a model in which hypertension arises from the convergence of blood pressure regulatory mechanisms, chronic inflammation, cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tissue-specific endocrine or vascular responses, with many of these enrichments showing very strong statistical support across 18 to 93 associated proteins.
